## Where This Fits
**Part III begins here. We now have recognition (Week 7), synthesis (Weeks 8–9), representations and tokens (Weeks 5–6), and a front end that removes what is not the user (Week 10). This week joins them into one model.** The most direct way to join them is Week 1's cascade: a recogniser, a language model and a synthesiser that pass only text to one another. Week 1 listed what the cascade discards — tone of voice, emotion, speaker identity, laughter, timing — and its three latencies add up. Remove the text interface, let one language model take speech in and give speech out, and what was discarded comes back. But once the text is gone, the model's command of meaning falls much further than anyone expected. **Every usable audio-native language model since 2023 is therefore an answer to one question: where does the text go — what do we lose by removing it, and what do we pay for keeping it?** That question runs through the whole week.

This week is restricted to **half-duplex** dialogue: the user finishes a turn, then the model answers; while the model speaks it does not process new input. Listening and speaking on one time axis is left to Week 12 (when to speak) and Week 13 (how an architecture listens and speaks at once). Half duplex comes first because every component of a full-duplex model — how speech enters a language model, how text and speech are ordered, how codec tokens are generated — must already be settled here, with one fewer variable. Note that stopping playback when a voice activity detector fires is still half duplex.

**Text can sit in five places**, and the week visits them in order of how far the text has retreated. (0) **The cascade**: text is the only interface between three complete models. (1) **Absent**: textless spoken language models (GSLM, AudioLM) do next-token prediction over speech tokens alone. (2) **In the weights and at the output only**: an encoder and an adapter connect speech to a text language model (SALMONN, the Qwen-Audio family; Week 7's LLM-based recogniser is the special case that only transcribes) — the model can hear but answers in text. (3) **Text first, speech after**, within one response; the variants differ in how closely speech follows: the whole text before any sound (chain of modality), a short span of text then a short span of speech (interleaving), a text stream aligned to every audio frame (Moshi's Inner Monologue), or two models, the second reading the first one's hidden states (Thinker–Talker). (4) **Text that is never spoken**: reasoning is text for the model's own use, and where it is placed in time decides how long the user waits. These are not five generations. Almost every public system in 2026 sits in (3); (1) remains the only route for languages without a widely used orthography; and (0) still frequently wins on semantic benchmarks.

**Keeping the text has two prices, one for each half of the lecture.** The first is paid in *ability*. After speech is connected to a text language model, the same question is often answered worse when spoken than when typed. This is the **modality gap**, and it cannot be blamed on recognition errors: models that transcribe the question correctly still answer it wrongly. It is a finding, not a law: the model in our own Demo 2, on the questions written for this course, showed none. It decomposes into forgetting of text abilities during adaptation and misalignment between speech and text representations. A less intuitive point: spoken input should let the model know *more* (tone, speaker, environment), yet in measurements models often perceive these cues without using them to change the answer. The second price is paid in *time*: however far the text leads the speech, that is how long the user waits. Writing the whole answer first is most accurate and slowest; frame-level alignment is fastest but needs word-level timestamps in training; and reasoning text is silent, so placed before the answer it is simply a pause — which is why recent work moves it to while the model is still speaking, or while it is still listening.

On the three course axes. **Representation:** input and output use *different* representations for the first time — most 2025–2026 systems listen with continuous features and speak with discrete tokens. Listening needs no sampling, and quantisation only discards information; speaking needs a distribution to sample from, which discrete tokens provide. Both sides have converged near 12.5 Hz for one reason: the language model's sequence length. **Latency:** several cells of Week 1's budget merge or vanish (the recogniser's tail; the language model's first token and the synthesiser's first packet become one cell), but the largest cell, endpoint detection, is untouched — a half-duplex model still waits for an external decision that the user has finished. That is the entrance to Week 12. **Supervision:** for the first time, ability comes from *other models*: meaning from text pretraining, dialogue data largely from synthesis, and text–speech alignment from a recogniser's timestamps. The modules of earlier weeks have not disappeared; they have moved into the training pipeline.

For the local languages, three points of different strength. For Taiwanese Hokkien, "where does the text go" becomes "which text": the best-known textless application is English–Hokkien speech translation for a language without a standard writing system, and even that work reports using Mandarin text as additional supervision. Audio-native models inherit their language coverage from their text model and their synthesiser; a first attempt exists for Taiwanese Mandarin, we know of no end-to-end dialogue model for Hokkien or Hakka, and the practical state is a cascade. Whether lexical tone survives the output tokens is supported by some evidence for Mandarin and by none for Hokkien; for Hokkien it remains a prediction.

## Learning Objectives
1. Draw the five places text can occupy in a spoken dialogue system (the interface of a cascade; absent; in the weights and at the output only; text first and speech after, in four variants; unspoken reasoning) and state for each what it preserves and what it costs in meaning, paralinguistic information, latency and alignment data.
2. Use token-rate arithmetic to explain the semantic ceiling of speech-only language models, and distinguish what each of three kinds of evidence supports: warm-starting from a text model, scaling analyses, and ablations that add a text stream.
3. Explain how speech enters a text language model (encoder, adapter, continuous vectors); define the modality gap and decompose it into forgetting and misalignment; design the four conditions that measure it (the original model reading text, the adapted model reading text, the adapted model hearing speech, and a cascade); and explain why the gap is not a recognition error.
4. Explain why training on the text model's own responses reduces forgetting, and why an audio language model answers from its text prior when the acoustic evidence is weak (continuing Week 7's account of hallucination).
5. Compare four output-side designs — chain of modality, interleaving, a frame-aligned parallel text stream, and Thinker–Talker — in terms of training data, the mismatch between training and use, and latency; and explain why systems listen with continuous features but speak with discrete tokens.
6. Write the response-latency expression of a half-duplex speech-to-speech model; identify which cells of the cascade's budget merge and which remain; derive from the interleaving ratio the two conditions "text must stay ahead" and real-time generation; and explain why latency figures from different papers are not directly comparable.
7. Design a "think before speaking" data format and compute the silence it costs; compare moving the reasoning into speaking time, into listening time, or into latent states; compute the context consumed by a 30-minute conversation under different representations; and name three structural limits of half duplex.

## Demos
The demos are programs and are published so that you can read them, re-run them, and change them — **you are not required to run anything**. Each folder's `README.md` gives requirements, setup, commands, and what you should see; the index at [`demos/`](https://github.com/hungshinlee/Speech-AI/tree/main/demos) explains the shared environments. Nothing is trained this week: every model is used for inference only. Demo 2's code is not published yet — its spoken Mandarin questions are still being fixed, and it has not been rehearsed.

## References
**Overviews (the backbone reading for this week)**
- Arora et al. (10 authors), **On The Landscape of Spoken Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey**, *Transactions on Machine Learning Research*, 2025 (arXiv:2504.08528) — organised as speech-only LMs, speech-plus-text LMs and speech-aware text LMs, the closest to this week's "where does the text go"
- Cui et al. (8 authors), **Recent Advances in Speech Language Models: A Survey**, ACL 2025, pp. 13943–13970 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.682; arXiv:2410.03751)
- Ji et al. (19 authors), **WavChat: A Survey of Spoken Dialogue Models**, arXiv:2411.13577 (2024; preprint)
- Peng et al. (12 authors), **A Survey on Speech Large Language Models for Understanding**, *IEEE Journal of Selected Topics in Signal Processing* (DOI 10.1109/JSTSP.2025.3640535; arXiv:2410.18908) — the listening side only

**What the cascade costs**
- OpenAI, **Hello GPT-4o** (13 May 2024; a company blog post, **not a paper**) — reports average latencies of 2.8 s and 5.4 s for the earlier three-model voice pipeline, describes what that pipeline loses (tone, multiple speakers, background sound; no laughter or singing in the output), and gives 232 ms minimum and 320 ms average for GPT-4o's audio responses. These are vendor figures with no stated measurement protocol

**Speech-only language models**
- Lakhotia et al. (11 authors), **On Generative Spoken Language Modeling from Raw Audio** (GSLM), *TACL* 9:1336–1354, 2021 (DOI 10.1162/tacl_a_00430; arXiv:2102.01192; also cited in Week 5) — speech-to-unit, unit language model, unit-to-speech
- Kharitonov et al. (11 authors), **Text-Free Prosody-Aware Generative Spoken Language Modeling** (pGSLM), ACL 2022, pp. 8666–8681 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2022.acl-long.593; arXiv:2109.03264) — separate streams for duration and F0 alongside the units
- Borsos et al. (11 authors), **AudioLM: A Language Modeling Approach to Audio Generation**, *IEEE/ACM TASLP* 31:2523–2533, 2023 (DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2023.3288409; arXiv:2209.03143) — semantic and acoustic tokens modelled in three stages
- Hassid et al. (12 authors), **Textually Pretrained Speech Language Models** (TWIST), NeurIPS 2023 (arXiv:2305.13009) — warm-starting from a text language model; both model scale and data scale matter
- Cuervo & Marxer, **Scaling Properties of Speech Language Models**, EMNLP 2024 (DOI 10.18653/v1/2024.emnlp-main.21; arXiv:2404.00685) — linguistic performance scales up to three orders of magnitude more slowly than for text models; coarser tokens made it worse
- Maimon, Hassid, Roth & Adi, **Scaling Analysis of Interleaved Speech-Text Language Models**, COLM 2025 (arXiv:2504.02398) — interleaved models scale more efficiently with compute than textless ones
- Sugiura, Kurita, Oda & Higashinaka, **Llama-Mimi: Exploring the Limits of Flattened Speech Language Modeling**, arXiv:2509.14882 (2025; preprint) — a single Transformer over flattened multi-level Mimi tokens; more levels improve audio quality and reduce content quality
- Park et al. (6 authors), **Long-Form Speech Generation with Spoken Language Models** (SpeechSSM), ICML 2025 (arXiv:2412.18603) — textless models lose coherence past tens of seconds; a state-space model generates many minutes in one decoding session
- Tseng et al. (5 authors), **TASTE: Text-Aligned Speech Tokenization and Embedding for Spoken Language Modeling**, ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2504.07053) — aligns speech tokens to text tokens at the tokenizer, bringing the sequence length down to that of text
- Chen et al. **Listening: speech into a text language model**

- Chu et al. (8 authors), **Qwen-Audio: Advancing Universal Audio Understanding via Unified Large-Scale Audio-Language Models**, arXiv:2311.07919 (2023; preprint); Chu et al. (12 authors), **Qwen2-Audio Technical Report**, arXiv:2407.10759 (2024; a technical report, not peer reviewed)
